text: This case involved a 17-year-old Pashto-speaking female who initially presented to a community emergency department (ED) after intentionally ingesting Ortho® Orthene Fire Ant Killer.
The ingestion occurred approximately two hours prior to the patient’s arrival at the ED.
The patient herself admitted the ingestion to her mother shortly after it occurred.
The patient’s father was called home from work and found the patient lethargic, diaphoretic, and with copious oral secretions.
Emergency medical services (EMS) were called.
At the time of the patient’s initial presentation, it was reported that she ingested approximately one half of the bottle (∼ 170 g).
The bottle accompanied the patient to the ED via EMS and was indeed noted to be half empty (Fig.

1); however, later in her course the patient clarified that she only ingested one “spoonful." In the ED, the patient had a temperature of 35.6 °C, blood pressure 116/67 mmHg, heart rate 129 beats per minute, and a respiratory rate 19 breaths per minute with an oxygen saturation of 98% on room air.
On examination, the patient was noted to be lethargic and minimally responsive to questioning.
She also had copious oral secretions, generalized weakness, and muscle fasciculations.
She had no bronchorrhea or bronchospasm.

Laboratory studies were largely unremarkable, aside from a slight leukocytosis (13.1 K/mcl), hyperglycemia (146 mg/dL), hypokalemia (3.0 mmol/L), hypomagnesemia (1.8 mg/dL), mildly decreased serum bicarbonate (19 mmol/L), and elevated INR (1.4).

A 67-year-old female patient was found by emergency medical services (EMS) smoking a cigarette outside her apartment approximately 30 min after a suicide attempt involving the ingestion of multiple medications, including but not limited to: metoprolol, nifedipine, nortriptyline, venlafaxine, and temazepam, all at toxic doses (a comprehensive list of the reported medications, their dosages, and mechanisms of action can be found in Table 1).
After ingestion, the patient contacted psychiatric services to convey a farewell message, leading to EMS being alerted.
Her medical history was notable for depression, iron deficiency anaemia, hypertension, reduced renal function attributed to previous lithium use, and prior suicide attempts.
Her estimated bodyweight was 90 kg.
At EMS arrival, she was hemodynamically stable with normal vital signs.
45 min after ingestion and during EMS transport, the patient deteriorated from full responsiveness with stable vitals to decreased mental status (E2M5V2).
On reassessment patient was tachycardic at 115 bpm, with a blood pressure of 86/48 mmHg, a respiratory rate of 10 breaths/min and an oxygen saturation of 92% on room air.
The patient presented at the emergency department (ED) approximately one hour after ingesting the overdose.
Her condition had already worsened significantly during transport and continued to deteriorate in the ED.
Ten minutes after arrival, her manual blood pressure readings were nearly unmeasurable, occasionally recording 50/30 mmHg.
Her heart rate declined to 65 beats per minute.
Her consciousness dropped further to E1M1V1 at this stage.
Castleman disease exists on a spectrum of lymph node involvement and severity.
UCD typically presents as an enlarged mass in the mediastinum, which may be visually apparent or detected incidentally.
Most patients are asymptomatic, but some may present with symptoms related to compression of nearby anatomical structures.
Laboratory abnormalities can include hypergammaglobulinemia, elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), and anemia.

Up to 90% of UCD cases present with hyaline vascular (HV) histopathology, which is characterized by atrophic germinal centers circumscribed with concentric rings of lymphocytes in an ‘onion-ring’ pattern and containing dysplastic follicular dendritic cells; the germinal centers are penetrated by hyalinized vessels giving a ‘lollipop’ appearance.
Unlike UCD, MCD is almost always symptomatic.
Patients present with multifocal lymphadenopathy and signs of systemic inflammation, most commonly fever, night sweats, fluid retention, and renal dysfunction.
These symptoms can be episodic, progressive, or chronic, and in severe cases can be fatal if left untreated.
Laboratory tests often reveal cytopenias, abnormal liver function tests, markedly elevated C-reactive protein (CRP) and ESR, and proteinuria.
The histopathology of MCD is more varied than UCD; it may present with a hypervascular type (hyperV), the plasmacytic (PC) type, or a mixed type.
The hyperV nomenclature is used to differentiate vascular MCD from HV UCD, though HV MCD and HyperV MCD are often used interchangeably by many authors.

The lymph nodes in the PC type are characterized by hypertrophic germinal centers, with intrafollicular spaces populated by sheets of plasma cells and vascular proliferations; as its name suggests, the mixed type exhibit features of both the HyperV and PC types.
The proband, a 60-year-old male, presented to our department on January 17, 2024, with a 5-year history of elevated serum creatinine (110–160 μmol/L) and persistent proteinuria (1–2+).
His medical history included long-standing hypertension and gout (duration >10 years).
Notably, his family history was significant, with both his father and maternal aunt succumbing to uremia (Figure 1).
Physical examination was unremarkable.
The laboratory workup revealed 2+ proteinuria without hematuria, with elevated 24-h urine protein excretion of 1.1 g/24h (normal range: 0–0.15 g/24h).

Serum biochemistry demonstrated normal albumin (40.5 g/L; reference 40–55 g/L), elevated creatinine (153.4 μmol/L; reference 57–111 μmol/L), and normal uric acid levels (221 μmol/L; reference 208–428 μmol/L1).
Immunological profiles showed normal IgG/IgA/IgM, C3/C4 complement levels, and negative autoantibodies (ANA, dsDNA, anti-PLA2R, ANCA).
Infectious disease screening was negative for HBV, HCV, HIV, syphilis, HSV, and CMV, with normal hematologic, coagulation, and thyroid function parameters.
Ophthalmologic examination demonstrated no anterior lenticonus or perimacular dot/fleck retinopathy, while audiometry showed no bilateral high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss.
Renal ultrasound revealed normal-sized kidneys with altered parenchymal echogenicity and a 2.0 × 1.6 cm right renal cyst.
On light microscopy, histopathological examination showed tubulointerstitial fibrosis, tubular atrophy with cystic dilatation, and global glomerulosclerosis (53%).
Immunofluorescence was negative for immunoglobulins and complement.

A 12-year-old Hispanic female with well-controlled systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis (sJIA) complicated by hypertension, posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome, and acute anterior uveitis, on biweekly tocilizumab, was referred to the nephrology clinic for persistent proteinuria.
She was diagnosed with sJIA in 2022 and was in clinical remission on tocilizumab several months later.
Proteinuria was first noted in 2023, 1.5 years after diagnosis of sJIA and 11 months into a state of clinically inactive disease.
She was referred to nephrology for proteinuria in 2024 with urine protein-to-creatinine ratio (UPC) ranging from 1 to 1.5 mg/mg (normal < 0.2 g/g) and a normal albumin of 4 g/dL.
She had no microscopic hematuria, and her serum creatinine was normal at 0.49 mg/dL with an estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) of 104.5 mL/min/1.73 m2 using the CKiD U25 equation.
She was normotensive with a blood pressure of 99/70.
Serologic workup was largely unremarkable aside from a positive antinuclear antibody titer (ANA) at 1:640 and a mildly low C3 level at 73 mg/dL (reference range 93–203 mg/dL).
At the time of presentation with proteinuria, the patient’s sJIA was clinically inactive, with no fevers, rash, or arthritis, and normal inflammatory markers (ESR/CRP).
Initial kidney biopsy revealed mild C3GN versus latent infection-related GN.
The sample contained 15–22 glomeruli, of which 1–3 were globally sclerosed.
The remaining glomeruli showed mild segmental mesangial hypercellularity.
Focal mild interstitial fibrosis and tubular atrophy (IFTA) were seen without significant interstitial inflammation.
We had three cases of fetal kidneys with T2-hyperintense cortex and T2-hypointense medulla reversal of the correct appearance.
In all of them, the kidneys were enlarged and hyperechoic on US of the second or third trimester, and the inverted pattern of cortex and medulla was only found on MRI.

All fetuses had enlarged kidneys on MRI performed between 32 and 36 weeks (range 52–58 mm), weaker diffusion restriction in the kidneys than under normal conditions, had their bladders filled, and no oligohydramnios/anhydramnios.
Figure 1 presents the MRI findings in fetus no.
1 compared with normal appearance of the fetal kidneys and with postnatal sonographic appearance.

The array comparative genomic hybridization (aCGH) analysis of the DNA extracted from uncultured amniocytes showed the deletion at 17q12 region ~ 1.4 Mb in size encompassing the region of renal cysts and diabetes (RCAD) syndrome (OMIM 137920, ORPHA: 93111).
The deletion included 15 protein-coding genes, including the HNF1B gene.
So far, no parental examination has been performed to assess the origin of the deletion of 17q12.

An eight-month-old male infant was referred to our center with the clinical diagnosis of prenatal onset Bartter syndrome, severe polyuria, advanced CKD, and poor response to treatment with sodium chloride and potassium chloride supplements, associated with ibuprofen first or indomethacin later.
Initial genetic testing for SLC12A1, KCNJ1, BSND, CLCNKA, CLCNKB, MAGED2, and SLC12A3 genes was negative.

Further diagnostic work-up including a panel of additional genes associated with hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis (CASR, KCNJ10, SCNN1B, SCNN1G, SCN4A, CLCN5, OCRL1, HNF1B, SCNN1A, NR3C2) turned out to be also negative.
He was the 2nd child from consanguineous parents, without a record of family kidney diseases, born after cesarean delivery at 34 weeks of gestation complicated by polyhydramnios since the 29th week.
He was born with normal weight and length for age (Table 1), and normal physical exam except significant hypotonia.
After birth, he presented early and severe polyuria (7 mL/kg/day), associated with severe metabolic alkalosis, hyponatremia, and hypochloremia of renal origin, but normocalciuria.
Other findings included remarkable hyperuricemia, mild hypercalcemia (2.84 mmol/L), and hypermagnesemia (1.28 mmol/L) associated with severe kidney dysfunction (Table 1).
Initially, kidney ultrasound was reported as normal.
No extrarenal manifestations were observed.

He was treated with high fluids and electrolyte supplementation (up to 28.4 mmoL/kg/day of NaCl and up to 196 ml/kg/day of fluids), and transiently discharged home at 1.5 months of life with enteral feeding.
He continued with polyuria and suffered from several episodes of hyponatremic, hypochloremic, and hypokalemic severe metabolic alkalosis, and progressive CKD (Table 1).

Repeated ultrasound at 4 months of age showed that both kidneys were small, at the lower normal range for age, with diffuse cortical echogenicity lack of corticomedullary differentiation, without nephrocalcinosis.
A 77-year-old man with a history of distal gastrectomy with Roux-en-Y reconstruction for gastric cancer presented with fever, general fatigue, and dysarthria.
Brain magnetic resonance imaging revealed acute cerebral infarction.
Blood cultures grew Streptococcus oralis, and echocardiography demonstrated vegetations on the mitral valve, leading to the diagnosis of IE.
Because the vegetation showed low mobility and mitral regurgitation was not severe, conservative treatment with intravenous antibiotic therapy was initiated.
Approximately 1 month later, the patient developed lower back pain, and lumbar magnetic resonance imaging revealed pyogenic spondylodiscitis (Fig 1).
Concurrently, rapid morphological changes were observed in a previously diagnosed AAA, leading to the diagnosis of infected AAA with impending rupture (Fig 2).
Inflammatory markers had normalized, and blood cultures had become negative, indicating clinical control of IE.
Semiurgent surgical intervention for the infected AAA was required.
However, the adjacent untreated spinal infection was considered to pose a high risk of graft reinfection.
Therefore, a single-stage multidisciplinary surgical approach was planned.
Because the patient had previously undergone robot-assisted distal gastrectomy with Roux-en-Y reconstruction, the availability of the greater omentum for graft coverage was uncertain.
Therefore, alternative reconstructive options, including a rectus abdominis muscle flap, were considered preoperatively.
A 70-year-old male presented to the hospital with intermittent ache and swelling in his right foot.
The patient claimed he had had the pain for several years and had difficulty standing and walking.
The pain worsened during the night and was alleviated with nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs).
There was no history of concomitant trauma.
The pain was localized in the head of the fifth metatarsal.
In physical examination, the distal diaphysis was tender and swollen without erythema and calor (Fig.
Range of motion (RoM) was intact, and there were no signs of neurovascular defects.
Initially, standard dorsoplantar (AP) and lateral radiographs of the foot were obtained.
In general, there was no sign of fracture or dislocation with normal overall alignment.
In lateral view, a small cyst-like lesion was seen (Fig.
Further imaging of the fifth metatarsal showed subtle cortical thickening along the shaft and a small lytic lesion in the axial view of computed tomography (Fig.

A 32-year-old woman presented with a two-year history of progressively worsening bilateral lateral calf pain associated with dysesthesia.
The symptoms were exertional in nature, initially occurring after prolonged walking but gradually progressing to occur after walking distances as short as approximately 90 meters.
The patient also reported symptom exacerbation with prolonged standing.
Symptoms were consistently relieved with rest.
The patient had no significant past medical or surgical history.
There was no family history of neuromuscular, connective tissue or peripheral nerve disorders.
She denied lower back pain, lower limb trauma and previous lower limb surgery.
There was no history suggestive of vascular claudication.
Clinical examination demonstrated altered sensation over the anterolateral aspects of both lower legs.
Motor examination revealed no weakness and there was no evidence of foot drop.
Dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses were palpable and symmetrical bilaterally.
No palpable masses were identified in either calf at rest.
A 62 years old man was referred to the Interventional Radiology Department for an internal/external biliary drain exchange, on a background of unresectable duodenal adenocarcinoma.

The locally invasive neoplasm involved the first part of the duodenum (D1) and extended into the common bile duct and the right hepatic duct, thus requiring a palliative internal/external biliary drain.
The procedure was performed under fluoroscopy with a plan for routine exchange of an indwelling 8.5 French Cook internal/external biliary drain (Cook Medical, Bloomington, IN).
A control image was obtained to assess the position of the indwelling drain.
An Advantage Glidewire with a hydrophilic tip (Terumo Corp., Somerset, NJ) was placed through the indwelling drain into the duodenum and the internal/external drain was removed over the wire.
A new 8.5 French drain was subsequently placed over the wire with its distal tip in the duodenum (Fig.
During the procedure, the distal locking pigtail loop appeared to be mispositioned in the third part of the duodenum (Fig.
2) and proximal retraction of the drain was performed.

Increased resistance was felt during retraction, and retraction was halted to allow a repeat contrast injection to assess the drain position which was then appropriately positioned in the second part of the duodenum.

Subsequent contrast injection demonstrated a 3 cm filling defect within the third part of the duodenum with evidence of obstruction of contrast flow beyond this area, the features of which were recognized as an intussusception (Fig.
The intussusception was presumed to result from traction of the catheter tip on the inner mucosa during proximal positioning.
Notably, the mechanism of this case differs from typical antegrade intussusception, as the tip of the catheter pulled the distal bowel proximally.
A 2-year-old Nauruan girl with known beta-ketothiolase (T2) deficiency presented to our institution with acute metabolic decompensation and encephalopathy.

Seventeen months before the current admission, at the age of approximately 7 months, the patient had been hospitalized at an overseas center with an episode of depressed consciousness following an upper respiratory tract infection.
At that time, she was noted to have tachypnea and decreased responsiveness.
Laboratory evaluation revealed severe metabolic acidosis with markedly elevated anion gap and strong ketonuria; lactate was not significantly elevated.
An inborn error of metabolism was suspected.
Because of concern for infectious or inflammatory encephalitis or demyelinating disease, a brain MRI was obtained.
That MRI demonstrated normal brain parenchyma, without abnormal T2/FLAIR hyperintensity, no restricted diffusion, and no abnormal enhancement.
There was no evidence of encephalitis, demyelination, or a primary metabolic leukoencephalopathy.
No basal ganglia, brainstem, or cerebellar signal abnormalities were identified at that time (Fig.
Given the unexplained severe ketoacidosis and normal structural MRI, a comprehensive metabolic and genetic evaluation was pursued.

Urine organic acid analysis showed a pattern consistent with an organic acidemia; subsequent extended genetic testing identified homozygosity for the I323V mutation in the acetyl-CoA acetyltransferase 1 (ACAT1) gene.
This I323V variant has been well established as a pathogenic mutation causing beta-ketothiolase deficiency.

A man in his 60s had swelling in his left inguinal region up to the left breech for 7 years since noticing the mass for the first time, which had grown rapidly for the past 3 months.
His medical history included appendicitis, a subarachnoid hemorrhage, and hypertension.
Marginal excision under general anesthesia was performed at a previous medical facility.
Histopathological examination confirmed that the mass was a squamous cell carcinoma, and the surgical margin was positive.
Therefore, the patient was referred to our hospital, and additional wide resection were performed.
Preoperative magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) from the previous hospital demonstrated a multilocular cystic tumor measuring 11 × 7 cm from the left inguinal region to the left breech.
Most lesions showed a high signal intensity on T2-weighted images (T2WI), with low signal intensity nodular lesions observed along the wall (Fig.
The nodular lesions appeared as iso-intensity signal to muscle on T1-weighted images (T1WI) and demonstrated contrast enhancement (Figs.
On diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) and ADC map, the entire lesion exhibited a high and low signal intensity, respectively (Figs.
The pathological findings of the resected tumor reveal squamous cell carcinoma with marked keratinization is observed.
A 23-year-old unmarried woman with regular menstrual cycles presented with a painless swelling in the left axilla that had been gradually increasing over the past 5 months.
She denied any history of trauma, infection, or previous breast or axillary surgery.
Her medical, surgical, and family histories were unremarkable.
On physical examination, a well-defined, mobile, nontender mass was palpable in the left axillary region.
The overlying skin showed no erythema, dimpling, or tethering, and there was no nipple retraction or discharge.
Examination of both breasts was otherwise unremarkable, with no palpable masses or lymphadenopathy on the contralateral side.
On ultrasound, the left axillary lesion was an oval, heterogeneously hypoechoic mass located 3-4 mm deep to the skin and oriented parallel to the skin surface.
The margins were macrolobulated with an angular upper margin, and no posterior acoustic features were present.
A central echogenic line within the lesion initially raised the possibility of an enlarged lymph node.

Taking these features together with interval growth over 5 months and the atypical axillary location, the lesion was categorized as BI-RADS 3 (probably benign), and ultrasound-guided core needle biopsy was performed to establish a definitive diagnosis and exclude nodal pathology (Fig.
Two additional nodules were noted in the breast, at the 1 and 4 o’clock positions.
Both were well-circumscribed, hypoechoic, and avascular, in keeping with incidental probably benign fibroadenomas, and both have remained stable in size on follow-up, consistent with a benign course.
An 8-year-old child presented to Nauru Medical Center with cough and failure to thrive.
The child was born to a 36-year-old G3P3 mother via normal vaginal delivery after a previous cesarean section.

Shortly after birth, the infant developed neonatal cyanosis, which initially resolved but later recurred, resulting in a 3-month admission to the neonatal intensive care unit, where oxygen therapy was required.
At the age of 3 months, a CT scan of the chest suggested the presence of only a functioning left lung.
During early childhood, the patient was considered medically fragile and required home oxygen therapy until the age of 2 years.
Despite early concerns regarding possible long-term disability, the child achieved all developmental milestones appropriately.
Since the age of 2 years, the patient has remained clinically stable, with no hospital admissions and only 1-2 minor respiratory illnesses per year, which were managed in the outpatient department.
The child currently attends regular school and is in Grade 2.
The parents reported a history of recurrent respiratory infections since infancy, occasionally associated with symptoms suggestive of cardiac failure.
These episodes required hospitalization on 1 occasion for 1 month, during which the patient was treated conservatively.
Before the arrival of a new medical team from GMSS, Nauru Medical Center did not have specialist medical services available.
The parents denied any history of tuberculosis, hepatitis, or other chronic infectious diseases.
A 58-year-old man presented with recurrent bleeding from a permanent ileal conduit urostomy.
His medical history was notable for bladder and prostate cancer treated with cystoprostatectomy and ileal conduit urinary diversion 2 years prior to presentation.

Additional comorbidities included obesity (BMI 37 kg/m²), chronic kidney disease stage 3, prior venous thromboembolism on anticoagulation, and cirrhosis secondary to metabolic dysfunction–associated steatohepatitis (MASH) with ongoing alcohol use.

The patient experienced multiple hospital admissions over an 18-month period for recurrent episodes of gross hematuria via the urostomy, resulting in symptomatic anemia requiring repeated blood transfusions.
He described steady, nonpulsatile bleeding from the stoma associated with fatigue and dyspnea.
Social history was significant for continued alcohol consumption of approximately 3-6 beers daily with heavier intake on weekends.
On examination, the patient was hemodynamically stable (blood pressure 127/79 mmHg, heart rate 84 bpm).
The urostomy appliance contained gross blood.
There was no ascites, jaundice, or hepatic encephalopathy.
Laboratory evaluation demonstrated severe anemia (hemoglobin 6.8 g/dL), preserved hepatic synthetic function (albumin 3.9 g/dL, INR 1.1), and chronic kidney disease (creatinine 2.0 mg/dL).
The Model for end-stage liver disease (MELD) score was 12, and Child–Pugh class was A.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated hepatic steatosis, mild splenomegaly, and prominent stomal venous collaterals extending from the right superficial inferior epigastric vein to the ileal conduit, consistent with stomal varices (Fig.
A 62-year-old man visited his local physician with a 2-day history of persistent headache and nausea.
Neurological examination revealed no focal deficits.
Plain computed tomography (CT) of the head showed subarachnoid hemorrhage and subcortical hemorrhage predominantly in the left frontal lobe (Fig.
1A), and he was transferred to our hospital under the careful management of blood pressure.
Three-dimensional CT angiography showed dilated cortical veins with varix extending from the left olfactory fossa to adjacent to the hematoma (Fig.

Cerebral angiography of the left external carotid artery showed a cortical vein with a varix draining into the superior sagittal sinus via the facial and ethmoidal arteries, forming a shunt at the olfactory fossa (Fig.
We diagnosed anterior cranial fossa dAVF, with the bleeding point considered to be the varix.
Right internal carotid angiography also showed severe stenosis of the middle cerebral artery with the developed moyamoya vessels (Fig.

Left internal carotid angiography showed stenosis from the terminal portion of the internal carotid artery to the M1 and A1 segments, with the development of moyamoya vessels in the surrounding area (Fig.
The patient had vascular risk factors associated with atherosclerosis, including hypertension and diabetes mellitus.

However, thin-slice T2-weighted MRI demonstrated shrinkage of the outer vessel diameter in the bilateral middle cerebral arteries and the terminal portion of the right internal carotid artery, findings that have been regarded as characteristic of moyamoya disease (Fig.
No other cause of arterial stenosis, such as vasculitis, was identified.

We present the case of a 45-year-old female with a past medical history of asthma and lactose intolerance who presented with bilateral hand numbness, migraines, neck pain, and left upper extremity pain.
The patient described the neck pain as a sharp pain radiating down the left arm into the hand.
The left upper extremity pain was positional and got worse at night.
This started gradually but had been going on for about 5 months.
On physical exam, the patient had upright posture with no visual deformity on inspection.
There was tenderness on the cervical spine with limited flexion and extension of the neck.
A positive Spurling test was observed on the left side.
A positive Tinel sign was noted on median nerve compression testing bilaterally.
The patient had a positive Adson and Roos test concerning for thoracic outlet syndrome as well as a positive Cozen’s test on the left elbow signifying lateral epicondylitis.

Radiographic imaging of the cervical spine demonstrated fusion anomalies and hemivertebrae in the lower cervical and upper thoracic spine (consistent with a type II Klippel–Feil deformity) with mild superimposed degenerative changes (Fig.

MRI of the cervical spine was obtained to better characterize the neurovascular structures associated with the fusion anomalies and to identify a focal source for the thoracic outlet syndrome symptoms.
MRI clarified the anatomical relationships of the fusion anomalies and hemivertebrae.

A 71 year old male with a past medical history of atrial fibrillation, mild nonobstructive coronary artery disease, hypercholesteremia, prediabetes, no smoking history, and severe symptomatic aortic valve stenosis with an ejection fraction of 60%, a valve area 0.8 cm², a mean gradient of 40 mmHg, and peak velocity of 4.5 m/s, presented with progressively worsening dyspnea on exertion for evaluation for transcatheter valve replacement (TAVR).
He denied chest pain, syncope, palpitations, however endorsed activity fatigue and dyspnea.
He had a history of radiofrequency ablation for atrial fibrillation and the placement of a permanent pacemaker.
Family history was noncontributory for congenital or premature cardiovascular disease.
Patient medications included aspirin, apixaban, and pravastatin.
On a physical exam, blood pressure was 144 / 85 mmHg, heart rate was 76 beats per minute, and oxygen saturation was 95% on room air.
There was additionally presence of a systolic murmur on auscultation, with the remainder of the exam within normal limits.
Routine laboratory evaluation was not contributory.
Due to the symptomatic aortic stenosis, the patient underwent a chest CT angiogram for pre-procedural evaluation for TAVR.
On TAVR CTA, a bicuspid aortic valve was identified, along with a 4.3 cm ascending aortic aneurysm and a 4.4 cm sinus of Valsalva aneurysm involving the noncoronary sinus.
Most notably, CTA imaging demonstrated an incomplete membranous band in the left atrium along the interatrial septum/fossa ovalis, consistent with cor triatriatum sinister (Fig.

A 17 year old boy presented with chief complaints of poor urinary stream, straining, intermittency and overflow incontinence for 2 months.
The boy had no prior history of hematuria or lower urinary tract symptoms.
Examination revealed a palpable bladder that failed to recede completely following voiding.
The external genitalia were normal and neurological examination didn’t reveal any abnormality.
The initial ultrasound (USG) examination showed thick walled urinary bladder with significant post-void residual urine.
The upper urinary tract was normal however a pedunculated polypoidal mass measuring 3×4cm was documented on the posterior bladder wall near neck (Fig.
The color doppler study revealed vascularity within the lesion and demonstrated its descent into prostatic urethra on voiding maneuver.
Retrograde urethrography revealed a normal urethra with a smooth filling defect near the bladder neck.
On voiding cystourethrography the same filling defect was seen to migrate into the posterior urethra (Fig.
Patient was planned for cystoscopic examination under general anesthesia.
Cystoscopy revealed a polypoidal growth (4×3cm) with long stalk arising from the bladder neck on left side and completely blocking the bladder neck.

A 76-year-old man with hypertension, hyperlipidemia, prediabetes, and presented as a trauma transfer after a rollover motor vehicle collision.

Initial evaluation at an outside hospital revealed bilateral rib fractures, a T10-T12 ligamentous injury with associated fluid collection, bilateral pneumothoraces requiring chest tube placement, and significant agitation requiring endotracheal intubation.
He was subsequently transferred to our facility for higher-level neurosurgical care.
Upon arrival, the patient was admitted to the surgical intensive care unit for management of a 6 mm subdural vs epidural hematoma, thoracic spine injury, and respiratory failure.
He remained intubated and sedated and was hemodynamically stable.
On hospital day 3, ultrasound-guided right subclavian vein access was attempted using a standard 18-gauge introducer needle, and a 0.035-inch guidewire was advanced.
Following placement of a 7F triple-lumen central venous catheter, arterial-appearing blood return was noted, and transduction confirmed arterial waveforms.
Given the presence of a large-bore catheter within a noncompressible arterial location, the catheter was left in place to tamponade the arteriotomy and avoid uncontrolled hemorrhage.

Computed tomography angiography of the chest confirmed direct cannulation of the lateral aspect of the distal brachiocephalic (innominate) artery, with the catheter tip extending into the aortic arch and a moderate mediastinal hematoma.
No pseudoaneurysm or active extravasation was identified (Fig 1, A).

Given that the catheter entry site was located on the lateral aspect of the artery approximately 1 cm proximal to the carotid-subclavian bifurcation, simple catheter removal with manual pressure would be at high risk of uncontrolled hemorrhage into the mediastinum.
Achieving an adequate endovascular seal would require covered stents deployed in a “kissing” configuration.
A 40-year-old female presented with productive cough, shortness of breath, pleuritic chest pain, and fever.

She reported a long history of recurrent respiratory symptoms beginning at the age of 17 years, characterized by repeated episodes of productive cough requiring multiple courses of antibiotics, which resulted in temporary improvement followed by recurrence within two to three months.
The patient also reported a history of primary infertility, with no prior successful pregnancies despite prolonged periods of unprotected intercourse.
There was no history suggestive of chronic sinusitis or imaging findings to suggest sinusitis (Fig.
The patient had not previously been diagnosed with Kartagener syndrome or primary ciliary dyskinesia.
Prior management consisted of repeated courses of antibiotics and symptomatic treatment for recurrent lower respiratory tract infections at various healthcare facilities.
Despite longstanding respiratory symptoms beginning in adolescence, no prior investigation for an underlying ciliary motility disorder had been performed.
The current presentation at 40 years of age represented the first recognition of the constellation of findings suggestive of Kartagener syndrome.
Computed tomography of the chest revealed dextrocardia with complete situs inversus (Fig.
There was bilateral bronchiectasis predominantly involving the middle lobe and lingula, associated with bronchial wall thickening and mucus impaction.
In addition, multiple areas of tree-in-bud nodularity were noted, consistent with small airway inflammation, along with patchy ground-glass opacities in the adjacent lung parenchyma (Fig.

The constellation of imaging findings, in conjunction with the clinical history of recurrent respiratory infections and infertility, was highly suggestive of an underlying ciliary motility disorder consistent with an atypical presentation of Kartagener syndrome.

A 52-year-old man with a history of arterial hypertension and chronic respiratory failure due to combined pulmonary fibrosis and emphysema (CPFE) syndrome, on home oxygen therapy for 1 year, presented to the Emergency Department of the Military Hospital of Tunis, Tunisia with sudden-onset right brachial monoparesis, faciobrachial paresthesia, and slurred speech lasting for 2 days.
He had a 52 pack-year smoking history and a previous ischemic stroke in 2022, for which he had been prescribed aspirin but discontinued it on his own.
The patient was admitted to the Department of Neurology of the Military Hospital of Tunis, Tunisia.
On neurological examination, the patient had dysarthria, right brachial monoparesis, and cerebellar ataxia.
The National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale (NIHSS) score was 5.
The modified Rankin Score (mRS) was 3 at admission.
A non-contrast brain CT revealed sequelae of a prior right superficial middle cerebral artery infarct and spontaneous hyperdensity of intracranial vessels (Fig.
Brain MRI with MR angiography showed an acute left paramedian pontine infarct without evidence of atherosclerosis (Fig.
Echo-Doppler of the supra-aortic trunks revealed a dominant right vertebral artery.

White blood cell count was 13,800/µL, and platelet count was 263,000/µL.

A 21-year-old male presented with complaints of progressive behavioral changes over the preceding several months.

According to his family, the patient developed increased irritability, mood swings, social withdrawal, and decline in academic performance, which were markedly different from his baseline personality.
He also exhibited psychiatric manifestations, including emotional instability and inappropriate behavior, for which he initially sought psychiatric consultation.
Over the following weeks, the patient developed tremors involving both hands, more pronounced during voluntary movements and fine motor tasks such as writing and eating.
The tremors were insidious in onset and gradually progressive.
There was no history of seizures, loss of consciousness, focal neurological deficits, headache, or visual disturbances.
The patient reported generalized fatigue and reduced appetite but denied jaundice, abdominal distension, hematemesis, melena, or pedal edema.
There was no history of alcohol intake, illicit drug use, or exposure to hepatotoxic medications.
Past medical history was unremarkable, and there was no similar illness in family members.
Preliminary investigations elsewhere revealed altered liver function tests, prompting referral for further evaluation.
On general physical examination, the patient was conscious and oriented, with stable vital signs.
Mild scleral icterus was noted.
A previously healthy 4-year-old boy presented to the emergency department with intermittent abdominal pain and episodic non-bilious vomiting of several weeks’ duration.
The pain was colicky, recurrent, and poorly localized.
There was no history of fever, weight loss, trauma, prior abdominal surgery, or exposure to livestock or unpasteurized dairy products.
On examination, the patient was hemodynamically stable.
The abdomen was mildly distended but soft, without guarding or rebound tenderness.
No palpable mass was identified.
Laboratory investigations were largely unremarkable.
The white blood cell count was within normal limits without leukocytosis.
Mild anemia was noted on subsequent testing.
Platelet count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and serum electrolytes were within normal limits.
Tumor markers (AFP and β-hCG) were normal.
Echinococcus serology was negative.

A 58-year-old woman with a past medical history of uncomplicated sigmoid diverticulitis treated medically in the past and remote caesarean section, presented to the emergency department with 3 days of left lower quadrant pain.
An imaging and interventional overview of the patient’s hospital course can be reviewed in Fig.
An IV contrast enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis in portal venous phase with coronal and sagittal reconstruction was obtained, employing iterative dose reduction technique (CECT).
This demonstrated acute perforated sigmoid diverticulitis without abscess.
The patient was admitted for IV antibiotics, fluids and pain control, and discharged the next day.
However, the patient continued to have gradually increasing pain, and prompted by new fecal urgency, returned to ED 2 days after discharge.
On examination, the patient was tender to palpation in the LLQ without rebound, and afebrile with white cell count (WCC) of 10.

Portal venous phase CECT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed a 3 cm collection contiguous with inflamed sigmoid diverticula, involving the ovary and a gas-filled serpiginous structure, the left fallopian tube (Fig.
This was consistent with perforated sigmoid diverticulitis with abscess and the rare finding of pneumosalpinx.
The patient was admitted to surgery.
Interventional radiology was enlisted to drain the collection on the day of admission.
Nonenhanced CT biopsy was conducted.

A 51-year-old male with a complex medical history including common variable immunodeficiency (CVID), hepatic steatosis, and prior total parenteral nutrition (TPN) use, presented for evaluation of chronic liver enzyme elevation and imaging findings concerning for cirrhosis.
Abdominal CT and MRI revealed nodularity of the hepatic surface and cirrhotic morphology, prompting further assessment to determine the underlying etiology (Fig.
The differential diagnosis included metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH), CVID-related hepatopathy, and TPN-associated hepatic injury.
Based on recommendations from hepatology, a liver biopsy was performed to obtain tissue for diagnosis.
An ultrasound-guided random liver biopsy targeting the left hepatic lobe was performed in the interventional radiology suite (Fig.
Moderate sedation was administered using fentanyl and midazolam, along with local lidocaine anesthesia.
The procedure was technically successful, with placement of an 18-gauge coaxial biopsy needle and retrieval of 3 core samples.
Minimal blood loss was observed (<15 mL), and no immediate procedural complications were noted.
Postprocedural tract embolization was performed with Gelfoam slurry to minimize bleeding risk.
However, within minutes of biopsy completion, the patient developed severe epigastric and right upper quadrant abdominal pain accompanied by chills and clinical signs of jaundice.
A postprocedural CT scan was performed in the portal venous phase, demonstrating cirrhotic liver morphology with heterogeneous enhancement of the left hepatic lobe in the biopsy region.

The observed heterogeneous left lobe enhancement was interpreted as a transient hepatic attenuation difference (THAD) reflecting compensatory arterial inflow in response to focal portal venous obstruction, rather than true parenchymal ischemia or infarction (Fig.

A 38-year-old man originally from Mozambique and living in Portugal for several years, with known HIV and HBV infections under regular follow-up, presented with a 2-month history of painless gross hematuria.
He denied dysuria, flank pain, fever, weight loss, recent travel to endemic areas, or prior urologic procedures, and there was no known history of urolithiasis or tuberculosis.
On physical examination, vital signs were stable and abdominal and genitourinary examinations were unremarkable.
Baseline laboratory tests showed normal hemoglobin, leukocyte, and platelet counts, with preserved renal function.
Urinalysis confirmed hematuria and leukocyturia without significant proteinuria.
Multiple urine specimens were examined for Schistosoma ova using standard microscopy, and all were negative.
A Schistosoma-specific PCR assay on urine was also negative.
Because hematuria persisted in an at-risk individual and the initial laboratory work-up was inconclusive, cross-sectional imaging was requested.

Although ultrasonography is often used as an initial examination in endemic settings, CT was selected in this patient because it offers superior characterization of mural calcification and distal ureteral involvement, which were the main diagnostic considerations after nondiagnostic laboratory results.
Noncontrast CT of the abdomen and pelvis (Fig.
1) demonstrated striking circumferential calcification of the entire bladder wall, extending into both distal ureters, resulting in an “eggshell” pattern of mural calcification.
Mild bladder wall thickening was present, but there was no intraluminal mass, hydronephrosis, or renal calculi.

Differential diagnosis at this time included intra-abdominal perforation, acute appendicitis, and colitis.

A 55-year-old Native American woman initially presented at age 33 to an outside emergency department for abdominal pain.
CT imaging at that time demonstrated mild hepatosplenomegaly and diffuse bony sclerosis (images not available, noting these images were obtained over 2 decades ago).
Blood work revealed thrombocytopenia.
The patient was referred to our facility for further evaluation.

At our center, the patient had a reported history of osteoporosis and degenerative joint disease of the hips, status post bilateral total hip arthroplasties (THA), the first performed as a teenager and the second as a young adult.
No surgical pathology reports are available from these THA procedures performed at an outside hospital over 3 decades ago.
At our institution, the diagnosis of adult-onset osteopetrosis was established based on clinical history, imaging findings, bone marrow core biopsy results, and peripheral blood smear results.
CT and radiographs demonstrated dense marbled appearance of the long bones and pelvis, sclerotic changes of the medullary space, and vertebral body deformities (Fig.

Analysis of the bone marrow core biopsy was difficult due to poor sampling secondary to sclerotic bone; however, pathologic evaluation reported foci of hematopoiesis consisting of erythroid precursors, maturing myeloid elements, scattered megakaryocytes, and plasma cells.

Peripheral blood smear was more consistent with a myelophthisic process, demonstrating leukoerythroblastosis, occasional teardrop and nucleated red blood cells, mild granulocytic left shift, and normal platelet count with occasional large forms which can be seen in states of increased peripheral platelet turnover.

Although the peripheral smear supported an underlying myelophthisic process related to osteopetrosis, the episodic isolated thrombocytopenia with preservation of other cell lines raised concern for a concomitant immune-mediated thrombocytopenia.
The patient’s platelet counts dropped as low as 3-4 × 10^3/µL multiple times, but each time, these counts responded to periodic treatment with a 4-day course of dexamethasone.
A 24-year-old woman with a history of type 1 diabetes mellitus on insulin therapy had been under ophthalmology follow-up for approximately 6 months due to diplopia.

Clinical examination revealed papilledema, confirmed on fundoscopy, and left abducens nerve (cranial nerve VI) palsy.

Glycemic control had been well maintained, with glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) values ranging from 34 to 41 mmol/mol, making uncontrolled diabetes a less likely primary contributor to her neurological presentation.

1), with no evidence of mass effect, hydrocephalus, or other signs of raised intracranial pressure.
CT angiography revealed a diffusely small-caliber petrous segment of the right internal carotid artery compared with the contralateral side (Fig.

Bone-window evaluation of the skull base demonstrated narrowing of the right carotid canal measuring approximately 3.5 mm, compared with 5.1 mm on the left (Fig.

Follow-up imaging at the outside institution showed multiple peritoneal masses that were biopsied and found to be strumosis without atypia.
The timeline of important clinical events is outlined in Fig.
Four years after her initial symptoms, she presented to our institution for additional workup and treatment due to relocation.

MRI of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated multiple enhancing peritoneal and abdominal wall masses and a homogenously enhancing structure in the left adnexa which was favored to represent the ovary (Fig.
The abdominal wall masses were biopsied and demonstrated follicular thyroid tissue without atypia.
At this time, the patient had a markedly elevated thyroglobulin level of 4326 ng/mL (normal range 1.6-50 ng/mL).
An I-123 whole body scan utilizing 1.2mCi of I-123 was administered to the patient, who was placed on a low iodine diet prior to the exam.
The 24-hour uptake scan showed significant uptake in the thyroid, but no significant uptake in the multiple peritoneal and abdominal wall lesions.

A 12-year-old girl with no significant past medical history presented with a two-year history of asymmetric joint pain affecting the ankles, knees, shoulders, wrists, and metacarpophalangeal joints, associated with myalgia.

Laboratory studies showed positive antinuclear antibodies (ANA) and elevated inflammatory markers, including erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and C-reactive protein (CRP), consistent with a diagnosis of juvenile idiopathic arthritis.

Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed bilateral intraconal pseudotumoral orbital tissue infiltration, isointense on T1-weighted sequences with marked homogeneous enhancement following gadolinium administration (Fig.
The lesions were hypointense on T2-weighted sequences, with preserved optic nerve morphology and signal on CISS sequences (Fig.

These findings were consistent with grade III bilateral proptosis, more pronounced on the left, with preserved extraconal fat.
Orbital biopsy demonstrated dense lymphoplasmacytic infiltrates interspersed with collagen bundles, confirming a chronic inflammatory process consistent with orbital inflammatory pseudotumor (Fig.
The patient was treated with corticosteroids, resulting in significant clinical improvement and complete resolution of ocular symptoms.
A 63-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with acute retrosternal pain after emotional stress.
High-sensitivity cardiac troponin I was elevated at 617 ng/L, decreasing to 545 ng/L after 2 hours.

A repeat transthoracic echocardiogram performed at the cardiology department clarified the pattern as predominantly midventricular hypokinesia (Movie 1).

The examination was performed on a first-generation dual-source photon-counting CT scanner (NAEOTOM Alpha, Siemens Healthcare GmbH, Forchheim, Germany) using retrospective ECG-gating with ECG-based dose modulation.
The average heart rate during acquisition was 71 beats/min.
Before image acquisition, the patient received 2 doses of sublingual nitroglycerin for coronary vasodilation.
No beta-blocker was administered.
Coronary arteries were nonobstructive (Fig.

Multiphase functional analysis demonstrated a left ventricular ejection fraction of 48%, with akinesia predominantly involving the anterior midventricular wall and mild residual akinesia of the inferior midventricular wall, while basal and apical segments contracted normally.
A man in his 50s presented to the emergency department with worsening anterior chest pain.
He had intermittently experienced anterior chest pain for approximately 4-5 years.

The pain was described as a pressing sensation and became more severe with physical activity.

Height: 180 cm; weight: 77 kg.
Body temperature was 36.6°C.
Pulse rate was 84 beats/min with regular sinus rhythm.

At the time of initial detection, he reported mild, intermittent left upper quadrant discomfort that resolved spontaneously within approximately one hour, without associated gastrointestinal or systemic symptoms.
His medical history included hypertension, hyperuricemia, and previous repair of a right inguinal hernia.

Laboratory tests showed mild elevations in several inflammatory markers, including fibrinogen, serum amyloid A, and high-sensitivity C-reactive protein.
Liver enzyme levels, albumin, and creatine kinase were slightly below the reference ranges, and tumor marker levels were normal.
Initial ultrasonography showed a hypoechoic mass in the spleen with an irregular but relatively well-circumscribed margin and scant internal vascularity on color Doppler imaging (Fig.
On unenhanced CT, the lesion appeared heterogeneous and hypoattenuating (Fig.

2); unlike its sonographic appearance, lesion margins were indistinct from the adjacent splenic parenchyma, likely owing to the limited attenuation difference between the tumor and surrounding parenchyma on unenhanced images.On contrast-enhanced CT, the mass showed avid but heterogeneous enhancement in the arterial phase, with focal hypoenhancing areas (Fig.
3).Enhancement decreased mildly in the venous phase but remained heterogeneous (Fig.

A 14-year-old girl presented to the emergency department with acute abdominal pain and peritonitis.
Notably, she has a personal history of TSC and seizures.
She has a family history of TSC with multiple siblings and father diagnosed with the condition; however, they were not afflicted with an arterial pathology.
On physical examination, there were multiple hyperpigmented macules, ash leaf spots, fascial fibromas, and extremity fibromas.
The abdomen was diffusely tender with focal peritonitis along the midline with an obvious pulsatile mass.
Vital signs showed tachycardia to 120 beats per minute, hypertension (180/90 mm Hg), and adequate oxygenation on room air.
Her vascular examination was intact with bilateral palpable femoral, radial, and pedal pulses.
Axial and coronal computed tomography angiography demonstrated an isolated 7.2-cm retroperitoneally contained a ruptured I-AAA (Fig 1, Fig 2, Fig 3).
Impulse control was promptly initiated to lessen further exsanguination risk and the patient was transported emergently to the operating room for open repair of the ruptured I-AAA.
Laparotomy revealed a 7.2-cm purely I-AAA with contained rupture into the retroperitoneum.
A transperitoneal approach was undertaken given the left lateral retroperitoneal nature of the rupture.
This strategy allowed appropriate aortic control distal to the bilateral renal arteries before aortic transection.

A 52-year-old male with a history of native bicuspid aortic valve with prior aortic valve replacement (25 mm Edwards Carpentier valve, in 2008) for group B streptococcal endocarditis presented to outpatient cardiology with 1 week of worsening shortness of breath.
He also reported chest tightness the day before presentation, but denied fever, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, edema, or constitutional symptoms.
On examination in the clinic, he was noted to have a new systolic murmur and was sent to the emergency room for further assessment.
Upon admission, vital signs were stable.
His examination revealed a loud systolic murmur but no signs of decompensated heart failure.

Laboratory workup showed elevated high-sensitivity troponins (86 pg/mL; repeat after 2 hours: 88 pg/mL) (reference normal range <20 pg/mL), brain natriuretic peptide (693 pg/ml; reference range 6-100 pg/ml), and d-dimer (1539 ng/mL; reference range 215-499 ng/mL).
His electrocardiogram showed nonspecific ST-T wave changes (T-wave inversions in leads I, aVL, and V4-V6), which were new compared with the prior ECG (Fig.
The patient was admitted with a diagnosis of non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI), and a left heart catheterization was performed, demonstrating normal coronaries (Video clip 1).
Chest X-ray and computed tomography pulmonary angiogram revealed bilateral pleural effusions and patchy ground-glass opacities but no pulmonary embolism.
The patient was admitted with a suspected NSTEMI and was on a heparin drip.
Further workup with transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE) showed left ventricular hypertrophy with mid-range left ventricular ejection fraction (45%-50%).

TTE showed a new intra-valvular leak of the bioprosthetic aortic valve compared with TTE a year prior, significant worsening of prosthetic aortic valve gradients (peak/mean 55/33 mmHg [26/17 mmHg 1 year prior]; aortic valve maximum velocity of 3.7 m/s, dimensionless velocity index of 0.27, and aortic acceleration time of 130 ms), and a dilated inferior vena cava (Video clip 2).
The patient is a 74-year-old woman who presented with a 1-month history of vaginal flatus and fecal-like discharge.
She reported no prior abdominal surgery, pelvic inflammatory disease, or malignancy.
Physical examination demonstrated mild lower abdominal tenderness but no palpable masses.
The patient denied recent trauma and reported no systemic symptoms, including fever, worsening abdominal pain, or unintentional weight loss.
Blood tests revealed elevated inflammatory markers, and vaginal microbiota analysis showed alterations in the microbial flora and acidic environment.
Transvaginal ultrasound (Mindray endocavitary probe) demonstrated an anteverted uterus with well-defined margins and normal dimensions.
Multiple gas-like hyperechoic foci were visualized within the uterine cavity, extending from the fundus to the internal cervical os (Video Editing S1 and S2).
The myometrium in the left uterine wall exhibited a focal discontinuity, forming a 3 mm wide tract communicating with the adjacent sigmoid colon; the margins of this communication were ill-defined.
Dynamic observation revealed passage of intestinal gas through the tract into the uterine cavity, creating a mobile gas-fluid interface (Fig.
1 and Video Editing S3).
Color Doppler imaging showed a flickering signal within the fistula tract and rich intestinal blood flow, suggesting local inflammatory changes.
Ultrasound impression: Abnormal uterine–intestinal communication, suspicious for colouterine fistula.
This is a 42-year-old male who was involved in a motor vehicle collision.
At the scene, he was found in respiratory distress with a deep, irregular respiratory rate of twenty breaths per minute and a low Glasgow coma scale (GCS) score, likely due to alcohol intoxication.
Consequently, he was intubated at the scene and transported to the trauma room.

Upon examination in the trauma room, he had a GCS score of 2T/15, which indicated severe impairment, and bilateral 3 mm reactive pupils, suggesting initially intact brainstem function despite the severe condition.
Under the effects of a muscle relaxant and sedation, the chest examination revealed decreased air entry on the left side, while the FAST exam was negative.
A CT scan showed multiple left-sided rib fractures with underlying pulmonary contusions, mild hemothorax, and pneumothorax, with no abnormalities in the head CT scan (Fig.
1), abdomen, and pelvis.
The ethanol level was 65.1 mmol/l, reflecting significant intoxication at the time of the incident.
He was subsequently admitted to the trauma ICU.
A follow-up CT head the next day (Fig.
2) revealed a small extra-axial hematoma, a few scattered small hemorrhagic contusions, and minimal subarachnoid hemorrhage.
Due to persistent low GCS, an MRI on day 3 showed a diffuse axonal injury grade 3.

She has noted furthermore slightly higher body temperature and about 1 kg weight loss.

Laboratory tests revealed slightly elevated but stable IgM level, a newly elevated lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) (667 U/L, rising to 1122 U/L).
A Fluorodeoxyglucose Positron Emission Tomography (FDG-PET) scan was ordered to rule out transformation to malignant lymphoma or other malignancy.
Bone marrow biopsy was also obtained and subsequently Prednisolone and Rasburicase were started.
The FDG-PET scan demonstrated diffuse, marked bone marrow uptake of FDG, multiple lytic lesions, and mediastinal, left sided hilar, and supraclavicular lymphadenopathy (Fig.
Bone marrow pathology revealed an epithelial malignancy positive for TTF1.

Further molecular analysis by Next Generation Sequencing (NGS) identified EGFR exon 19 deletion (c.2235_2249del, p.E746_A750del) in combination with a nonsense mutation in TP53 exon 9 (c.949C>T, p.Q317*).
Careful review of the chest CT and PET imaging showed a possible primary tumor in the left upper lobe (LUL) (Fig.
Treatment with osimertinib was initiated, resulting in a complete metabolic response of FDG-PET scan (Fig.
The LUL lesion was evolved into a small, vague ground-glass opacity.
A 37-year-old male presented with progressive weakness in the lower limbs, which commenced two months before admission and later affected the upper limbs.
He reported observing a distinct mass in the right inguinal region.

On dermatologic examination, the only cutaneous abnormality identified was a newly developed erythematous papular lesion consistent with a red mole in the left axillary region, which had appeared about one month prior to admission.
Neurological imaging indicated a normal brain MRI, whereas the spinal MRI showed a lytic lesion in the L1 vertebral body extending into the left pedicle (Fig.
Moreover, there was notable thickening and contrast enhancement of the spinal nerve roots, especially in the cauda equina region and conus medullaris (Fig.

Abdominopelvic CT scan demonstrated multiple enhancing right inguinal lymphadenopathies and several lytic and sclerotic bony lesions (Fig.

The maximum short-axis diameter (SAD) recorded was 30 mm.
The ultrasound-guided biopsy of the inguinal lymphadenopathy confirmed the diagnosis of Castleman disease (mixed type).
The immunohistochemical analysis of the lymph node biopsy demonstrated CD20 positivity in germinal centers, signifying B-cell proliferation.
A 25-year-old woman presented for a routine fetal ultrasound examination at 18 weeks gestation.
Maternal medical history was unremarkable, with no known risk factors or medication exposure during pregnancy.
Ultrasound examination was performed using a 5 MHz curvilinear transducer with sagittal and axial imaging planes.
Color Doppler imaging was used to assess fetal venous flow patterns.
Imaging demonstrated normal anatomical relationship between the inferior vena cava (IVC) and aorta.
In the sagittal plane, the aorta coursed parallel to the spinal column, while the IVC followed a similar course to the level of the renal vessels.
Beyond this level, the IVC deviated anteriorly from the aorta, producing the IVC Takeoff Appearance (Fig.
Axial views supported this anatomical relationship, while color Doppler demonstrated normal venous within the IVC.

This case illustrates the typical appearance of the IVC Takeoff Appearance, supporting normal fetal systemic venous anatomy and serving as a practical educational landmark during prenatal ultrasound evaluation.
A 35-year-old primigravida presented for a late fetal anomaly scan at 28-weeks gestation.
Maternal history was unremarkable, with no known risk factors or medication exposure during pregnancy.
Ultrasound examination was performed using a 5 MHz curvilinear transducer with sagittal and axial imaging planes supplemented by color Doppler evaluation.
A 51-year-old male presented with complaints of abdominal pain for the past 1 month, which had progressively increased in severity and was not relieved by medications.
The pain was associated with nausea and vomiting.
He was a known case of hypertension for 1 year and diabetes mellitus for 5 years with a history of occasional alcohol intake over the past 20 years.
The patient also reported episodic headache, palpitations, and weight loss.
Routine blood investigations revealed elevated serum amylase (∼725 U/L) and serum lipase (∼583 U/L), along with raised total leukocyte count (∼19.9 × 10³/µL).
A diagnosis of acute pancreatitis was made, and the patient was referred to the radiology department for contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen to assess for complications of pancreatitis.
Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen performed on a 64-slice scanner revealed multiple cystic lesions in the liver, pancreas, and bilateral kidneys.
Imaging revealed near-complete replacement of pancreatic parenchyma with multiple variable-sized cystic lesions.

In addition, features of pancreatitis were present, including peripancreatic, perirenal, and bilateral paracolic gutter fat stranding with a few loculated collections in the lesser sac and perisplenic region.
Mild prominence of the pancreatic duct was noted without evidence of pancreatic calcification.

A provisional radiological diagnosis of acute-on-chronic pancreatitis with walled-off necrosis was made in the background of suspected VHL, with an associated mixed solid-cystic left adrenal lesion, likely representing a cystic pheochromocytoma.

Gore & Associates) was placed on the proximal side of the stent graft owing to suspicion of a type Ia endoleak.

Retrograde left iliac arteriography revealed blood flow into the aneurysm through the vascular plug (Fig.
A 65-year-old Iranian female arrived with stomach bloating, heaviness, and constipation as her early symptoms.

Other Imaging work-up of MRI with rectal-pelvic protocol revealed a well-circumscribed iso to high T1W and intermediate T2W in the ischioanal space, which seemed to be intramuscular without invasion to adjacent structures such as the rectum (Fig.

A 38-year-old man presented with a 3-month history of vague intermittent left flank pain.

1A was missed on initial USG).

Early venous phase CT images revealed a well-defined cystic lesion adjacent to the left renal pelvis and upper pole major calyx, without evidence of ureteral dilatation.
